## The problem

A CMO needed answers from existing marketing data to plan activities, without waiting on an analyst to pull and format a report every time. The system had to answer natural-language questions grounded in the company's own structured/tabular data — reliably enough to actually inform planning decisions, not just look good in a demo. [[TODO: one sentence on the specific data (campaign performance? spend by channel?) and the kind of planning decision it fed.]]

## The finding

```{python}
#| label: fig-hero
#| fig-cap: "Answer accuracy across question types, before vs. after retrieval grounding. Replace with your real eval."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

cats = ["lookup", "aggregation", "multi-table", "temporal"]
before = np.array([0.71, 0.52, 0.38, 0.44])
after  = np.array([0.94, 0.86, 0.72, 0.79])
x = np.arange(len(cats)); w = 0.38

BG, FG, MUTED, GRID = "#0e1016", "#f4f5f7", "#9aa3b2", "#22262f"
A1, A2 = "#6366f1", "#22d3ee"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
fig.patch.set_facecolor(BG); ax.set_facecolor(BG)
ax.bar(x - w/2, before, w, color=GRID, label="baseline LLM")
ax.bar(x + w/2, after,  w, color=A1, label="RAG + structured QA")
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(cats, color=MUTED)
ax.set_ylabel("answer accuracy", color=MUTED); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
ax.legend(frameon=False, labelcolor=FG)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(GRID); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(GRID)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor=BG)
plt.show()
```

The hard questions (multi-table, temporal) are where naive prompting fails — grounding in the actual retrieved data is what made those trustworthy. [[TODO: replace the numbers above with your real eval-set results — not in work history, needs your own records/GitHub.]]

## Decisions and tradeoffs

I split the problem into retrieval (grounding answers in the right context) and answer synthesis over structured data, rather than asking one prompt to do everything — that made each half testable and each failure debuggable. On the retrieval side, I compared semantic vs. sparse search rather than defaulting to one, since marketing questions mix fuzzy ("campaigns similar to...") and exact-match ("Q3 spend on...") lookups that favor different retrieval methods. ## Measurement and limitations

Evaluated on a fixed question set by answer accuracy [[TODO: size of the eval set, how you graded, latency/cost budget — not in work history]]. Limitations: degrades on data/tables the system hasn't seen, and retrieval quality bounds answer quality — a wrong or incomplete retrieval means a confidently wrong answer downstream. Worth noting for credibility: this took 2nd place in Tiger Analytics' internal hackathon rather than shipping to a live CMO in production — an internal build-off result, not a production deployment claim.
:::

## How it works

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the retrieve → answer flow (sketch)"
#| eval: false
# Replace with a readable slice of your real pipeline.
def answer(question: str) -> str:
    ctx = retrieve(question)            # semantic + sparse search over data
    return synthesize(question, ctx)    # LLM grounds its answer in ctx
```
